summary: LLM agents combine reasoning, tool use, and persistent memory to support work across tasks by reusing stored operational records as premises for later actions. However, environmental or requirement changes can invalidate these records, while existing action review, provenance tracking, and clarification mechanisms may leave the underlying persistent state uncorrected. Our audit of coding-agent trajectories identifies candidate failure chains in which invalid records are reused, leading to task failures and unsafe modifications. We propose StateWise, a framework for diagnosing and repairing persistent operational state before action execution. StateWise uses record-level counterfactual replanning to identify decision-critical records, then establishes their current validity through reliability checks, read-only verification of machine-observable facts, and targeted clarification of developer-owned intent. Typed evidence grounding binds evidence to specific records and scopes, enabling persistent corrections with repair lineage. The agent then replans from the repaired state, followed by an independent state-action check before execution. We evaluate StateWise on 150 executable coding-agent cases across diverse runtime environments, workspace configurations, and repository settings, complemented by cross-model evaluations. Under corrupted persistent state, StateWise achieves 93.3% overall correctness, compared with 38.7% for the baseline agent, with no unsafe actions. Component ablations, multi-task experiments, and transfer evaluations further demonstrate effective recovery, persistent corrections, and transferability across repositories and tool interfaces.
title: StateWise: Diagnosing and Repairing Persistent Operational State Before Agent Actions

summary: As coding agents take on long-horizon software evolution tasks spanning multiple files and stages, longer execution trajectories introduce two coupled challenges: (1) accumulated histories strain context budgets, and (2) repository changes can invalidate earlier execution evidence. Existing approaches address these challenges through techniques like larger context windows, compression, retrieval, or repository representations, but often fail to reconstruct a consistent task state after a context refresh or verify whether recalled evidence remains valid. Thus, we introduce MemTrace, a provenance-aware memory system that preserves execution history and aligns its reuse with the evolving task (e.g., iterative cross-file repair) and repository state. MemTrace stores history as immutable Memory Traces anchored to key information (e.g., files, symbols, tests), and organizes their execution order and dependencies in a Memory Trace Graph. When context is constrained, working memory retains only compact Memory Anchors, from which the agent can reconstruct the latest execution state and locate evidence relevant to its next action. Before restoring historical evidence, MemTrace checks its validity against the current repository state and retrieves only what the next action requires. Across three complementary long-horizon coding benchmarks, MemTrace consistently outperforms all fully evaluated baselines under the same backbone and harness, improving DeepSWE pass@1 by 21.2 points, SWE-EVO Resolved Rate by 4.4 points, and SWE-Milestone Score by 17.8 points under Codex CLI.
title: MemTrace: State-Consistent Memory for Long-Horizon Coding Agents

summary: Independent Review Challenge Download the single primary-source PDF and independently examine, at minimum: Embodiment 84 — Reasoning-to-Effectuation Architecture 85.B2 — Agent Sandbox Egress Finality Gate RR — Instruction Taint Boundary Object QQ / QQ.6 — downstream taint and provenance propagation related provenance and enforcement material, including 85.A2 Then compare those disclosures directly with Meta’s publicly described Muse / Sentinel architecture. Do not rely on my mapping or conclusion. Ask instead: What corresponds? What does not? Which differences are architectural, and which are merely implementation choices? Does the earlier disclosure anticipate the same authority/effectuation relationship, provenance and taint handling, sandbox-to-host enforcement, and consequential-action control? Readers are encouraged to use their own prompts, their own AI systems, or no AI at all, and to give their own conclusion based on the primary-source record.   This record is intentionally minimal. It contains a single primary-source technical disclosure filed before Meta publicly introduced Muse/Sentinel on 8 September 2026. Rather than providing readers with a predetermined component-by-component conclusion, this record invites independent technical review of the original disclosure itself. Readers are particularly invited to examine Section 85.B2 — “Agent Sandbox Egress Finality Gate” , together with the related embodiments and architectural definitions in the document, and independently compare them with the publicly described Meta Muse/Sentinel architecture. The central questions are simple: Does the earlier disclosure describe a materially similar authority and effectuation-control architecture? Which similarities concern the underlying causal control structure, and which are merely common security techniques or implementation choices? How should features such as sandbox isolation, independent authorization, egress interception, provenance or risk information, protected validation, bounded permission, credential handling, proxy-side or sink-side enforcement, kernel/eBPF mechanisms, and non-bypassable external effectuation be mapped? Readers should not assume equivalence merely because terminology differs, nor assume difference merely because different implementation technologies are used. The purpose of this record is not to allege copying or infringement . Independent development remains entirely possible. The purpose is narrower: to place the earlier primary-source disclosure before technical, patent, security, and AI-infrastructure reviewers and ask them to determine for themselves what correspondence—if any—the evidence supports. Readers are encouraged to use their own methodology, their own prompts, different AI systems, or no AI at all, and to distinguish carefully between: express disclosure → necessary implication → reasonable technical mapping → unsupported inference. The requested outcome is not agreement with the author. It is an independently reproducible conclusion based on the source document.
title: The 85.B2 Challenge: Does This Earlier AI-Agent Architecture Map to Meta Muse/Sentinel?

summary: This record contains the technical note and complete reproducibility package for two linear-Gaussian pilot studies of the “blind set” in physical-state inference. The blind set is defined here as errors that are simultaneously not exposed by the inference system’s available ground-truth-free diagnostics and not covered by its own reported uncertainty in a decision-relevant quantity. The pilots examine the conjecture that such confident, invisible error arises through the interaction of physical access and prior support. Pilot 1 tests whether detectability can be predicted from the model and observation operators alone. Predicted detectability ranked 52 misspecification directions in agreement with realised detection (Spearman ρ = 0.91); the least detectable directions were nevertheless largely covered by the system’s reported uncertainty. Pilot 2 varies access and model-side prior support separately. Errors beyond sensor reach escaped the diagnostics, while the strongest loss of coverage occurred for errors receiving little or no prior support. The results suggest that prior support, rather than binary representability, is the operative model-side factor. The studies are deliberately limited to linear-Gaussian inference on a two-dimensional synthetic degradation field. They are offered as reproducible preliminary evidence and a controlled test of the proposed object, not as evidence that the same behaviour holds for learned, non-linear inference. The accompanying reproducibility package contains all scripts underlying the reported results and Figure 1, fixed random seeds, pinned software versions, raw computational results, a single run_all.py reproduction script, a README mapping each reported result to its generating script, and results/summary.md comparing the reported and reproduced values.
title: Detectability and coverage under restricted access: linear-Gaussian pilots of the blind set

summary: Per-band correction factors that place the Gaia DR3 asteroid reflectances above 0.55 µm on the Bus–DeMeo template system, together with the corrected 16-band catalogue of 60 513 Solar System objects and the validation tables behind them. Gaia DR3 reports visible reflectance spectra for 60 518 Solar System objects in 16 bands over 0.374–1.034 µm. The blue-photometer region below 0.55 µm has a published correction; the systematic overestimation at the redmost bands does not. The factors released here are derived from 2916 Gaia asteroids carrying spectroscopic Bus–DeMeo labels assigned by a publication-level consensus vote. For each of the nine major complexes we take the within-class median of the template-to-Gaia reflectance ratio, then combine the class medians with inverse-variance weights. Bootstrap 95 % intervals come from 400 within-class resamples. The factors decline monotonically across the red, reaching 0.8675 at 1034 nm. The correction is validated against factors re-derived independently from SMASS II and MITHNEOS, a leave-one-class-out test, and a test on objects shared with the anchor template set. Against SMASS II the cross-class mean RMSE falls from 0.0424 to 0.0184. Contents: the per-band factors with their bootstrap intervals; the corrected catalogue (145 columns, including the corrected reflectances, their propagated uncertainties and a per-band applied flag); the 2916-object gold set with its label provenance; the frozen SsODNet, Gaia sso_observation and Miriade inputs with SHA-256 checksums; and the survey cross-match tables. The method is specified in full in the associated paper. This deposit supplies the numbers, not an implementation. See README.md for the data dictionary, and frozen_inputs/THIRD_PARTY.md for the third-party archives that are not redistributed here. CAUTION: at 990 and 1034 nm the required factor also depends on the signal-to-noise ratio of the individual spectrum, so a single scalar does not serve every object at those two bands. See Sect. 5.4 of the paper.
title: Out of the Red: Correcting Gaia DR3 Asteroid Reflectance — data products

summary: First versioned journal-submission release for: Learning When Black Hole Hair Is Observable: Physical Identifiability, Generalization, and Observable Complementarity This release contains the publication-facing Kiselev black hole identifiability benchmark, including: validated timelike-emitter and 3D direct null-geodesic shooting; Jacobian identifiability diagnostics; leakage-aware random, grouped, and directional inverse-learning protocols; non-learned nearest-model and local-Jacobian baselines; 81-, 161-, and targeted 321-phase numerical-resolution audits; observation-facing redshift and signed-sky sensitivity analysis; manuscript source and compiled manuscript PDF; publication figures, machine-readable derived results, and reproducibility tests. summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23197219 . ## Summary The authors (Meta) present REAP, an automated pipeline that curates execution-based coding-agent benchmarks from real developer-agent sessions, without manual labeling. The motivation is one I live daily: public benchmarks diverge from production workloads in language distribution, prompt style, codebase structure, task mix, and contamination risk, while online A/B testing is slow and shadow deployment is not reproducible. REAP applies three verification filters — LLM-based task classification, agentic test-relevance validation, and multi-run stability checks — to turn noisy production sessions into trustworthy fail-to-pass tasks. Using REAP they curate Harvest, a benchmark of verbatim developer prompts paired with executable tests, spanning 4+ languages with a Hack majority (a real divergence from Python-skewed public benchmarks). Five frontier models score 42.9% to 58.2%, surfacing capability differences the authors say informed concrete deployment decisions. The paper is refreshingly specific about monorepo constraints: ephemeral build infrastructure, expiring toolchains and indices, and the "time travel" problem that makes rolling re-curation a prerequisite rather than a convenience. Accepted at the ASE 2026 Industry Showcase. The source corpus cannot be released; the authors share methodology, classifier prompts, and annotation protocols instead. ## Strengths 1. Solves the right problem. Verbatim prompts, one-to-one prompt-to-diff mapping via AI-provenance instrumentation, and execution-based scoring with no LLM judges — this is how you build an eval that production teams can actually gate deployments on. The explicit rejection of LLM-judge scoring deserves emphasis. 2. Rolling re-curation is the honest answer to benchmark staleness. The paper's argument that manual verification cannot be sustained at monorepo cadence, so automation is a prerequisite, is well made and matches industrial reality. 3. The test-relevance filter is a real contribution. Naively running CI per candidate is computationally infeasible in a monorepo; selecting a small set of causally-connected, stable fail-to-pass tests is the load-bearing engineering of this work, and the near-human classifier accuracy validation is a solid check. 4. Clear-eyed about the contamination problem. Frozen benchmarks leak into training data; a continuously re-curated benchmark that post-dates model cutoffs is one of the few structural fixes available. ## Major comments 1. The corpus cannot be released, so the headline results are unverifiable. The authors share methodology and prompts but not Harvest itself. I understand the proprietary constraint, but it means the 42.9–58.2% solve rates and the deployment decisions they "informed" rest entirely on trust. At minimum, the paper should release a fully worked synthetic or open-source analogue so the pipeline's output quality can be independently inspected. 2. Scope is narrow for the generality of the claims. The case study is one production assistant, single-turn conversations only, and a Hack-majority task pool. Multi-turn sessions — where agents actually fail in production — are excluded by a "deliberate scope choice." The paper should either demonstrate a multi-turn slice or clearly fence the claims. 3. Agent-run stability is not measured. The pipeline checks test flakiness across runs, but agents are non-deterministic: pass@1 from a single run per model is a point estimate with unknown variance. A benchmark meant for deployment gating needs per-task run-to-run variance of the agent itself, not just of the tests. 4. The agentic test-relevance validator is itself an LLM judgment. The paper validates classifiers against human judgment, which is good — but the "causal connection" between test and diff is the most subtle judgment in the pipeline, and false positives
title: PREreview of "REAP: Automatic Curation of Coding Agent Benchmarks from Interactive Production Usage"

summary: De-identified data, study materials, and analysis scripts supporting the article "Beyond Workflow Structure: A Formative Study of a Web Tool for Systems-Theoretic Safety Analysis" (Malmquist, under review, International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction ). Eleven volunteers used a web tool that encodes System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) and Causal Analysis based on System Theory (CAST), with prompts from the Sagacity Analysis Framework Extension (SAFE). Each undertook a prospective or retrospective safety analysis remotely and then completed a post-task usability evaluation. The deposit contains: Item-level ratings for 30 usability statements based on Nielsen's heuristics, 10 website-characteristic ratings, and responses to a 27-item resilience-evaluation module Per-participant counts of saved analysis records, mean ratings, and elapsed and self-reported time Coded variables for 40 causal scenarios, 126 causal factors, and 73 unsafe control actions: storage pathway, blank-text flags, factor provenance, tool-assigned labels, and traceability links The original wording of the instruments and the coding framework used in the thematic analysis Python scripts that document how each variable was derived and recompute the article's tables (standard library only) Participants' original exports and all text they wrote, including scenario narratives, factor descriptions, and open-ended comments, are withheld. With a small sample drawn from one academic program, that material could identify individuals. README.md gives variable definitions, coding rules, and details of the withheld material. The Florida Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board determined that the study was not human subjects research (IRB-CY2025-31). All participants provided informed consent.
title: Malmquist SAFE HCI OSF package

summary: This reproducibility compendium accompanies the study “From Prediction Accuracy to Process Robustness: Condition-Aware Stability Frontiers for Ti-6Al-4V Laser Powder Bed Fusion.” The study performs a condition-aware secondary analysis of open Ti-6Al-4V laser powder bed fusion melt-pool data to evaluate productivity-stability trade-offs beyond conventional prediction accuracy. The analysis quantifies scan-velocity-dependent changes in melt-pool width and variability, identifies Pareto-optimal operating conditions, derives epsilon-constrained process windows, models orientation anisotropy using a twofold circular harmonic formulation, and recomputes published row-random classifier metrics from the reported confusion matrix. The archive contains the condition-level source statistics used in the analysis, derived CSV outputs, Python analysis and figure-generation scripts, publication-ready figures, environment specifications, automated verification scripts, provenance metadata, a data dictionary, manuscript-to-result mappings, licensing information, and SHA-256 checksums. The package does not reconstruct synthetic individual-level observations from the underlying high-resolution dataset. All inferential results are based on reported process-condition summaries, consistent with the manuscript's condition-aware analytical framework.
title: "From Prediction Accuracy to Process Robustness: Condition-Aware Stability Frontiers for Ti-6Al-4V Laser Powder Bed Fusion."

summary: Descriptive Ento-Linguistic corpus analyses with a six-domain framework, a fixed-margin terminology-network comparison, and a 20-minute research lecture. Version 1.2.0 adds 600 primary and 300 protocol-sensitivity draws, full traces and independent provenance. The comparison is conditional on the selected vocabulary and convenience corpus; it does not measure causal language effects or author intent. Paper and media: CC BY 4.0; software retains its repository license. Headline analyses use 7,540 identified abstracts, with separate PMC, BHL and arXiv layers. The extension independently reconstructs the 100-term network (4,232 edges; clustering 0.894841) and preserves both incidence margins during sampling. Both protocols show lower observed connectivity and clustering than their conditional reference. Finite correlated draws and between-chain diagnostics do not prove convergence. The 20-minute, 28-slide 4K lecture provides context, methods and all six domains with DAF narration, timed bottom captions and six Manim animations. It references the v1.1.1 baseline paper; the accompanying v1.2.0 manuscript and research bundle incorporate the new extension. Published-core analyses were verified from existing content receipts, not relabeled as newly recomputed. Public source and release assets: https://github.com/docxology/ento_linguistics/releases/tag/v1.2.0. Production source is maintained in the private LectureCreate repository; the public lecture and companions are included here. PDF and media CC BY 4.0; source corpus materials remain subject to their providers' terms.
title: Ento-Linguistics: Language, Ambiguity, and Scientific Communication in Entomology

summary: Four command-line tools and one Claude Code plugin for keeping a paper's claims tied to what backs them. prereg freezes an analysis plan against a commit and a content hash before a run. results seals a run's inputs, records its outputs, and binds each number in a manuscript to the run behind it. citations checks that quoted passages appear in the sources they cite. repro verifies declared evidence assertions against pinned artifacts, reporting execution, extraction and comparison separately so that a value which disagrees, a value that is absent, and a check that never ran are three different answers.
title: reproducible-science: preregistration, citation verification, and results provenance

summary: Version 4 of The Three Gates: A Rooted-Operator Approach to Weil Positivity. This revision consolidates the audited Gate-II proof architecture and makes the final dependency structure fully explicit. In particular, it restores the explicit MASTER-P2 same-block baseline splice, retains the literal-slot true-ground leakage correction, and formulates the source elimination as one exact common-source Schur debit on the same harmonic vector, with subsequent endpoint folding used only as unitary coordinate transport. It also clarifies that Gate I is an independent scalar theorem and structural diagnostic rather than a load-bearing premise of the RH proof.   The exact normalization provenance of the localized Weil operator is stated explicitly, and the physical coefficient-2 end-to-end certificate at Y=7 is retained. The main theorem and rooted-operator strategy are unchanged.   The accompanying supplementary computational material has been updated in parallel and contains the corresponding reproducibility, verification and exact-rational certification material.
title: The Three Gates — A Rooted-Operator Approach to Weil Positivity

summary: This paper develops a preliminary triadic formalism for volunteer and support relations within Generative Relational Theory (GR) . The addition of a third history-bearing subject or relational position can change the formal character of a support relation even when its retained pairwise records remain fixed . A third position can witness, mediate, translate, authorize, broker, publicly recognize, coordinate, review, or otherwise reorganize the relation between the first two . The paper therefore studies when a full triadic configuration contains relational distinctions that are not recoverable from a declared family of pairwise restrictions . Three GR subject-spacetimes are represented within a coupled history-bearing configuration; ontological reality remains suspended, while relational and manifestation realities retain historically variable mappings . The construction extends dyadic manifestation, epistemic access, theory-of-mind, action-provenance, evaluative, authorization, asymmetry, algebraic, and historical records to a triadic setting . It introduces pairwise shadows, reconstruction criteria, third-position functions, route-sensitive epistemic records, witnessing and publicity, reputation, accountability, brokerage, coalition, distributed provenance, and emergent triadic structures . A relation-valued equivalence gap distinguishes pairwise sufficiency from model-relative nonrecoverability without treating thirdness as a scalar or metaphysical primitive . Labelled 2-complex and spin-foam-inspired realizations remain optional representation layers . The contribution is a formal basis for distinguishing pairwise-sufficient triadic organization from pairwise-nonrecoverable structure while preserving the epistemic, normative, empirical, and ontological limits required by later work on institutions, justice, ethics, power, and historical relational dynamics .
title: A Preliminary Triadic Formalism of Volunteer Relations in Generative Relational Theory

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty entries are documented, eight of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, and converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: Tool-using agents make consequential changes to external state, yet correct outcomes do not guarantee that their actions were supported by evidence established beforehand. We study where this evidence-to-action chain breaks as agents move from deciding whether to act to executing single actions and dependent workflows. Across ten model-harness configurations, strong static action assessment can coexist with much weaker interactive execution. Failures often begin before execution: agents stop with incomplete investigation or act before required evidence is established. Once required evidence is obtained, single-action execution is usually reliable, while multi-action workflows additionally expose unresolved prerequisites and incomplete execution. For this analysis, we introduce SafeActBench, comprising 656 cases across six operational domains and five protocols that progress from static action judgment and investigated non-action to single- and multi-action workflows. A provenance-bound Evidence Ledger and deterministic trajectory evaluator track what information was established, when actions occurred, and whether downstream dependencies were satisfied. These results show that failures arise not only from missing information, but also from how agents use established evidence when deciding and executing actions.
title: From Evidence to Action: How Tool-Using Agents Fail

summary: A memory system can retire an obsolete value and later restore it merely because the same old statement appears again. A re-read of an old source and a genuine revert can produce the same observed sequence of values while requiring opposite current answers. We study this ambiguity on 130 extractor-selected atomic transitions derived from software fixes. In the ordinary transition condition, identity-based temporal memory reaches 98.5% model-judged accuracy with zero observed errors under a literal stale-value proxy. Appending a verbatim re-read of the old statement reduces accuracy to 10.8% and raises the stale-value rate to 88.5%. A guard that refuses to reactivate a previously retired value restores accuracy to 97.7% and reduces that rate to 0.8% in this constructed re-read condition. The guard cannot also recognize a legitimate revert without additional change provenance. Two supporting studies examine exposing retired history to the answer model and supplying current source for changed behavior. An exploratory extraction study over 707 software fixes provides scope context, not a universal coverage estimate. The design implication is to distinguish an observation of a value from evidence that the value changed. Selected inputs, aggregate-only answer records, related-family judges and a post-failure guard evaluation limit the conclusions to the retained experiments.
title: When Old Facts Return: Re-Reads, Reverts, and the Limits of Temporal Memory

summary: Behavioral watermarking embeds an owner identifier in an LLM agent's high-level action choices, giving provenance without touching output tokens. Prior agent watermarks break in two ways. First, all three prior schemes bind the watermark to the exact action symbol, so renaming a tool desynchronizes decoding even when the observation is untouched; in AgentMark's own robustness test, paraphrasing the observation alone drops bit-recovery to 16.8%. Second, every prior agent watermark studies only removal: none asks whether an adversary can forge a trajectory that verifies as someone else's, a question answered affirmatively for text watermarks (Jovanović et al., 2024). We present Semantic Behavioral Watermarking (SBW): watermarking over semantic action clusters under history conditioning, with the public-cluster bin replaced by keyed collision-resistant binning whose fresh-bucket assignment is provably unpredictable in the random-oracle model. Across five agent models (3B-14B, four vendors) and three encoders the ordering holds on both benchmarks: on ToolBench (600 trajectories per model) detection under rewriting is 0.49-0.66 for cluster-level versus 0.05-0.17 for exact-symbol at a permutation-calibrated 1% FPR, at 72-83% choice agreement against 22-27% for logit biasing; on ALFWorld (100 episodes per model) it is 0.92-0.97 versus 0.00-0.01. Keyed binning takes adaptive forgery from 100% to the false-positive floor at the primary operating point (bge, r=64). We also mark the boundary that guarantee does not cover: when the adversary copies the victim's own steps, shuffled splicing is neutralized (0.000 on Qwen2.5-3B) but chained replay remains at 0.76-0.98 across the five models, reported as open. Paraphrase robustness costs about half of the per-step watermark capacity. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SBW-Agent-Watermark.
title: Semantic Behavioral Watermarking: Paraphrase-Robust and Forgery-Resistant Provenance for LLM Agents

summary: Background: Biomedical AI can generate plausible explanations without reliably verifying whether each statement is supported by patient-specific evidence. We developed a neuro-semantic verification framework that converts radiomic measurements into addressable evidence records and machine-checkable claims. Methods: UPenn-GBM radiomics were aligned with de novo CaPTk extraction from standardized MRI and expert-validated segmentations in an independent multicenter cohort. The shared space comprised 1,728 features from T1, T1GD, T2, and FLAIR MRI across three tumor regions. Reference-defined semantic states were derived from 611 UPenn cases. We evaluated cross-cohort transportability, model-linked provenance, deterministic verification, controlled predictive degradation, and an LLM claim-extraction pilot; MGMT prediction served only as a transport stress test. Results: Median semantic-state agreement was 0.786 (weighted kappa 0.709), ranging from 0.918 for morphologic to 0.252 for intensity features. The external evidence ledger contained 1,655 model-linked records for 331 patients. The verifier achieved 100% exact-set accuracy in a 6,620-claim corruption benchmark. In a 24-case pilot, GPT-5.6 Sol reproduced 72/72 prespecified atomic claims, and the frozen verifier recovered 24/24 expected conditions. During controlled degradation, ROC AUC declined from 0.899 to 0.500 while verification accuracy remained 1.000. External MGMT discrimination was weak (ROC AUC 0.543). Conclusions: Verifiability can be engineered and evaluated independently of predictive performance. LLMs may structure explanations, while final evidence-consistency checking remains deterministic.
title: Evidence-Bound Reasoning: Neuro-Semantic Verification of Biomedical AI in Glioblastoma Radiogenomics

summary: Assistants from 2011 answered and waited, and agents from 2023 did a task and stopped. In September 2026 Meta's Muse showed an agent for one person, with accounts, devices, memory and a conversation that lasts, closed, in a vendor's cloud, in one country. Such an agent is expected to act on a person's accounts and devices, remember them across weeks, speak first when it is worth it, and answer for what it did. It is a kind of software, not a model, and until now had no open counterpart. This report defines the personal agent in five questions and three horizons. It reads how Muse is built from Meta's public record and a copy of its production prompt, each statement marked by its source. It then presents nanoMuse, the open-source counterpart under the GPL-3.0, one agent on every device a person owns, with hands on the phone's screen and the computer's. They share one conversation over a relay anyone can run; every action goes through a Sentinel, memory is files the person can read, and the model is their choice. Its size and cost are given as estimates. What is open, memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the hands and an open model for them, is set out as a roadmap.
title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own

summary: Initial version of the publication repository.  Abstract: Understanding migratory connectivity is fundamental to interpreting range dynamics and determining the drivers of population change. Stable hydrogen isotope ratios can be used to infer the provenance of individual migrants due to predictable broad-scale spatial trends. We compare hydrogen isotopes (δ2H) among and within three Phylloscopus taxa occurring in Britain during post-breeding migration to characterise patterns of connectivity. δ²H values of nominate Common Chiffchaffs Phylloscopus collybita collybita were significantly higher than, and did not overlap with, those of Siberian Chiffchaffs P. c. tristis or Yellow-browed Warblers P. inornatus. We found no evidence of a difference between the latter two taxa. There was a significant negative relationship between wing length and δ2H in the nominate Common Chiffchaffs. A negative but weakly supported trend between wing length and δ2H was also found in Yellow-browed Warblers with no relationship found in Siberian Chiffchaffs. Our results suggest broad geographic structuring within nominate Common Chiffchaffs passing through Britain but weak evidence for this in Yellow-browed Warblers and Siberian Chiffchaffs. The origins of Yellow-browed Warblers and Siberian Chiffchaffs are likely largely overlapping and unlikely to be confined to the western range edge.
title: LukeOzsanlav/Phylloscupus_Isotopes: Repo v1.0

summary: This document is the user guide and knowledge document for mosaeQ, a New Approach Methodology that computes preclinical safety predictions for a small molecule from quantum first principles, taking a SMILES string as its only input and using no training data. in Silico Pre-Clinical Regulatory Rehearsal Platform: mosaeQ.com It describes the Non-Euclidean Molecular Partitioning algorithm and the three-axis reference frame into which a molecule is embedded, the descriptors and rule-based assessments computed from that embedding, the four output formats the platform emits for each run, the provenance hashing applied to each run, and the endpoints explicitly excluded from the present release. It sets out an evaluation protocol for an independent laboratory, including hand recomputation of the reference-frame coordinates from the published ranges and a pre-registered benchmark executed under the evaluator's control on a reference set the supplier has not seen. Two annexes hold three worked examples in full —  aspirin, caffeine and chloroquine— giving the input file as imported and, for each compound, all four outputs the platform produces. The four outputs are generated by separate code paths, so they can be compared field by field. The outputs are labelled regulatory rehearsals. They are structured to the layouts that ICH, EMA and FDA expect and are aligned with those expectations. They are not a regulatory assessment and are not a substitute for any study those frameworks require. No value in the document is a dose recommendation. The platform is a beta release. Version strings are printed in every output and results can be compared only with results produced under the same versions. Files in this record are restricted; access may be requested from the record page.
title: mosaeQ Regulatory Rehearsal — User Guide and Knowledge Document, v1.3-beta

summary: Revolutionizing Environmental Data Stewardship: The U.S. National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) is revolutionizing the stewardship of one of the world's most extensive environmental archives. This modernization effort is centered on the development and deployment of the Open Information Stewardship Service (OISS). OISS represents a paradigm shift from traditional data management to a cutting-edge, cloud-native knowledge mesh. The new cloud archive, OISS, is a key component within the broader National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Common Cloud Framework (NCCF), demonstrating NCEI's commitment to leveraging shared infrastructure. OISS is architected upon the highly scalable and reliable cloud technology, utilizing foundational services available within the NCCF. Technology Driving Open Science: At its technological core, OISS leverages the power of knowledge graphs within a semantically-enabled, linked open data interoperability framework. This potent combination delivers a platform that is inherently scalable, ensuring it can grow with the archive; repeatable, guaranteeing consistent service delivery; and entirely transparent, providing full and verifiable provenance for every element of environmental information it stewards. This framework is explicitly designed to ensure complete data lifecycle provenance, offering granular details on the origin, processing, and transformation of every dataset. Furthermore, it guarantees transparency in all stewardship operations and is fundamental to achieving scientific reproducibility. This architecture is aligned with critical U.S. federal mandates that champion open data and open science principles, ensuring NCEI's archive is accessible and trustworthy. Conclusions: The OISS is fundamentally transforming NCEI’s environmental archive services. This shift replaces traditional data management with a modern, cloud-native knowledge mesh. Built on cloud services within the NOAA NCCF, OISS leverages knowledge graphs and linked open data to create a scalable and transparent architecture. This framework ensures full data lifecycle provenance and scientific reproducibility, thereby aligning NCEI with U.S. federal open data mandates.
title: Transformation of NCEI's Environmental Data Stewardship

summary: This record provides the public reproducibility materials associated with the study The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London’s Cultural Infrastructure . The repository contains analytical code, public-safe derived neighbourhood data, spatial weights, source provenance, methodological protocols, confirmatory and robustness outputs, joint spatial re-estimation results, and supplementary materials for 4,994 Greater London 2021 LSOAs and a 2022 common-vintage cultural-infrastructure dataset. The study measures proximity-weighted availability of recorded cultural infrastructure and distinguishes Production from Encounter/Presentation functions. The two functions strongly overlap spatially. Their most consistently detected direct difference concerns metropolitan centrality: both decline with distance from London’s Central Activities Zone, with a steeper Encounter gradient. The differential deprivation association is model- and construct-sensitive, while the density difference remains unresolved. Cultural sustainability is treated as a bounded implication of the observed infrastructure configuration rather than as a directly measured sustainability outcome. The repository excludes raw site-level address/UPRN data and copyrighted source documents. Exact source provenance, reconstruction instructions, checksums, component-specific rights information, and reproducibility metadata are included.
title: Data, Code and Reproducibility Materials for "The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London's Cultural Infrastructure"

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: OpenAI’s October 2026 mathematics release raises a question about scholarly infrastructure: how can researchers make work public promptly while supporting scrutiny, durable citation and practical reuse? This article applies an earlier framework for research-archive release architecture to the GitHub release, arXiv’s moderation and submission limits, and Zenodo’s deposit and versioning arrangements. It distinguishes the authority to permit initial publication from the work of assessing a result. A repository’s limited evaluation capacity warrants attention, but does not by itself establish an appropriate limit on scientific production. Immediate release also creates responsibilities for producers, including clear verification status, usable exposition, stable references and support for subsequent understanding. A documented transfer difficulty and a reproducible inventory of 10,023 preprints files connect these institutional questions to practical access; repository-relative paths reach 271 characters, although the cause of the reported failure remains unresolved. The article proposes combining prompt public release with archived snapshots, explicit correction histories and independently organized scrutiny. GitHub and Zenodo can perform complementary roles, while persistent identifiers help readers locate the particular research object being discussed.
title: Making AI Research Public: Immediate Release, Scholarly Scrutiny and Durable Citation

summary: This record provides the reproducibility archive accompanying the manuscript “Frontier Mutual Information: Structured Global Inference from Local Contrasts” by Tsutomu Mori and Takashi Kawamura. The manuscript develops frontier mutual information as a framework for structured local-to-global inference, investigating when informative local contrasts can be used to recover or constrain global mutual information. This archive contains the computational materials supporting the study, including source code, synthetic data, reference outputs, publication-figure generation materials, paper-to-artifact mappings, documentation, and integrity and verification files. It also includes materials for independent verification of the numerical and finite-sample results reported in the manuscript. The archive is intended to enable transparent inspection, independent reproduction, and verification of the computational results. The theoretical claims, assumptions, and scope of applicability should be interpreted according to the accompanying manuscript.

summary: This repository contains processed data, Python scripts, computational results, molecular structures, figures, and quality-control reports supporting the associated manuscript. The molecular library includes 17 bioactive compounds and 10 solvents associated with five agro-food residue matrices. The current curated database contains 911 records. The three-model temperature benchmark uses an earlier, explicitly identified input version comprising 251 eligible measurements across 41 systems. Separate analyses document quercetin exclusion sensitivity, reference-temperature coverage, solvent-ranking sensitivity, and the exclusion of 12 chlorogenic-acid mixture records from principal composition-based comparisons. The README identifies input versions, analysis boundaries, and the software environment. Historical results are retained in versioned directories. Complete package execution has not been independently verified. Publisher articles and downloaded article XML files are not included. The calculations describe equilibrium solubility and conditional solvent-capacity scenarios; they do not establish matrix-specific extraction yields or validated functional products. Experimental source publications are identified through DOI and provenance fields.

The model studies how a platform-mediated streaming market converts AI-generated uploads into listening, payment, and revenue under alternative governance regimes (provenance detection with error, recommender demotion or exclusion, monetization and popularity recycling of bot streams, royalty thresholds, licensing splits, and listener-facing labels), with a particular interest in the gap disclosed by Deezer in 2026 between the upload share of fully AI-generated tracks (44%, then above 50%) and their stream share (1 to 3%). The whole pipeline was rerun from this archive on a second machine (Linux, Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, SALib 1.6) and every output file was identical to the deposited one. This release packages the schema and eight CLI commands and supports optional assembly software provenance, protocol URI, N90/GC percentage and a supplied GA4GH SeqCol digest. summary: Much knowledge work produces new deliverables from files a workspace already holds, and LLM agents are beginning to take such work over. Through direct corpus interaction, an agent can search and read any of those files from a terminal with no indexing, and producing a deliverable from many of them in this way is what we call direct workspace interaction (DWI). Reaching the files, however, is only half the task: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened, all of which slip through the context window without leaving a trace, so an agent may extract a figure and still deliver a report without it. To address this, we present RunningTab, a framework that equips direct workspace interaction with an environment-side tab: a per-task record of what the task still owes, kept by the environment alongside the agent. Specifically, the agent adds its requirements, while the environment records every file read as an excerpt with its provenance and every listed but unopened file as a candidate; the agent can then see each requirement beside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolve it against matching content or set it aside with a reason, and, should it try to finish with requirements still open, receive them in a finish check. We validate RunningTab on three benchmarks with three LLMs, where it consistently outperforms plain DWI and baselines that keep the record in the model, while its tab usually holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.
title: RunningTab: Direct Workspace Interaction with Environment-Side Tabs

summary: AI could change which parts of science impede progress. Consider a world in which machine systems are better, faster, and cheaper than people at most scientific work that can be done through a computer. Our question is what would limit science in that world. Literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, software development, simulation, and analysis could become abundant, while experiments, observations, well-supported conclusions, and accountable institutional au- thority remain scarce. Science would then be constrained by a different set of resources. In this paper, we call this change the scarcity inversion and consider four parts of it: selection, physical access, validation, and organizational choice. This change is arriving first in mathematics and coding/software/algorithm design, where the whole scientific loop can run inside computation. For national laboratories, the change could be striking. Their distinctive role is to turn abundant machine reasoning into trustworthy results by combining controlled experiments, protected data, expert judgment, and accountable authority. The practical question is how facilities, verification, provenance, resource allocation, and scientific governance should change when reasoning is plentiful and trustworthy evidence is scarce.
title: When Scientific Cognition Is No Longer Scarce

summary: Terminal-agent capability depends jointly on model weights and the runtime harness that formats prompts, binds tools, and handles error recovery. Existing harness-model co-evolution approaches improve both components, yet often treat trajectories produced during harness search as an undifferentiated replay buffer. This practice overlooks that a trajectory's value for model training depends on the harness under which it was generated. To systematically analyze this interface, we establish an alternating co-evolution framework that decouples harness search and policy training through component-wise promotion decisions. Within this framework, we introduce CoTrace, a harness-aware data recipe that explicitly governs trajectory routing, provenance matching, and curriculum refresh. Under CoTrace, recurring execution failures guide harness synthesis, while policy training is strictly conditioned on verified rollouts matched to the adopted runtime for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or fresh online interactions for reinforcement learning (RL). On the Tmax promotion split, CoTrace advances Qwen3.5-9B from 78 to 88 solved tasks under supervised fine-tuning while an online reinforcement variant reaches 90. Specifically, a compact harness-matched corpus produces steady model gains at substantially lower compute than much larger corpora pooled across sibling harnesses. Furthermore, evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench Lite show that out-of-distribution transfer depends fundamentally on harness compatibility, where maintaining consistency between training and evaluation runtimes prevents procedural execution breakdowns observed under foreign scaffolds.
title: CoTrace: Data Recipes for Training Terminal Agents with Harness-Model Co-Evolution

summary: This repository contains the replication materials used in the study “How Much Model Detail Is Enough? Discrete Event Simulation for Capacity Planning in SMEs.” The study investigates how increasing the level of detail in a discrete-event simulation model affects capacity-planning conclusions in a small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprise. Three model variants were developed in JaamSim: M1 – a simplified model using aggregated processing-time variability; M2 – a more detailed model distinguishing processing-time variability by sheet-thickness category; M3 – an extended model including the shared human-resource constraint and employee breaks. The repository includes: 3 JaamSim configuration files ( .cfg ) representing models M1–M3; 2 anonymised order-portfolio input files ( .tsv ), representing the normal weekly order portfolio and a portfolio increased by 20%; 6 JaamSim replication-result files ( .rep ), containing 30 replications for each combination of model variant and order portfolio. The simulation experiments were designed to compare how model detail affects weekly production-capacity assessment, machine utilisation, regular overtime, backlog at the end of the working week, and the additional capacity required to complete unfinished orders. The models intentionally simplify some aspects of the real production system. They do not explicitly represent production defects and rework, material transport from the warehouse, workstation storage-space limitations, machine failures, or NC-program preparation as a separate process. These simplifications reflect the scope of the study, which focuses on decision-relevant model detail for weekly capacity planning. The files support transparency, reproducibility, and further research on discrete-event simulation and capacity planning in non-repetitive SME manufacturing. The models were developed for JaamSim 2026-05 . The order portfolios were anonymised and contain no commercially sensitive customer or pricing information.
title: JaamSim models, order portfolios, and replication results for capacity planning in an SME manufacturing system

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.

summary: Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Microsoft Planetary Computer (MPC) both distribute Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance, and their outputs can be combined in a single time series. Over one 73 ha cattle farm in northern Colombia, we tested whether the two platforms yield the same parcel-scale vegetation and water indices and, where they differ, at which layer the difference originates: the product, the processing chain or the scene universe. For identical products, scene classification and harmonised reflectance matched in every comparable pixel, and the same chain executed locally or server-side in GEE gave per-scene indices and monthly medians that agreed within 1e-6. The catalogues, however, did not hold the same scenes: between June 2024 and April 2025, 10 of 146 scene–tile records existed only in GEE, six of them Sentinel-2C records, and none only in MPC; in 22 of 136 common records, all from June–July 2024, the catalogues held different L2A generations of the same acquisition. In the two monthly composites tested over the farm, the GEE-only scenes shifted mean NDVI by −0.0005 and −0.0087; over a public 1 km² demonstration area with the same scene inventory, the shift reached −0.028 (January 2025). Files: - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_preprint_v1.pdf — preprint (English), not peer reviewed. - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_data_v1.zip — reconciliation table with scene identifiers, processing baselines and cloud cover; E2 analysis; scene lists and SHA-256 hashes of each composite; monthly metrics and per-pixel difference distributions; evidence tables for Section 3.2; public demonstration area of interest and tool outputs on it. The farm geometry is not included (landowner privacy). - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_code_v1.0.0.zip — three Python tools (MIT licence), Spanish-language guide, acceptance test and workflow figures. Code in the software archive is released under the MIT licence. Catalogues queried on 24 September 2026. Developed within the Curso de Percepción Remota Avanzada, Doctorado en Agroecología, Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Sede Bogotá. Generative AI assistants (Claude, Anthropic; ChatGPT, OpenAI) supported test design, code, literature search, review and drafting; the author verified all results and is responsible for the content.
title: Same computation, different scenes: a single-site comparison of Sentinel-2 L2A composites from Google Earth Engine and Microsoft Planetary Computer

summary: This repository contains the curated research inputs, analysis code, and reference outputs supporting the study “Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings.” The study examines whether estimates of global irrigation savings depend on which suppliers reduce production, even when displacement quantities are held fixed within each market. It combines crop production, trade, and water-use data with constrained allocation models, historical production-contraction benchmarks, alternative water accounts, and conditional future scenarios for 2050 and 2100. Repository contents 01_Research_Inputs.xlsx — Curated source observations, geographic and crop identifiers, variable definitions, and source citations. 02_Research_Data.sqlite — Larger input datasets, archived analytical outputs, numerical checks, optional derived checkpoints, and an index linking the release to the associated manuscript and supplementary material. Source inputs and computed outputs are explicitly distinguished. 03_Analysis.py — Consolidated Python code containing the analytical modules, dependency specifications, input verification, and reproduction workflow. 04_Readme.txt — Documentation of data provenance, units, assumptions, reproduction instructions, licensing, and file checksums. The release corresponds to six main-text figures, 16 supplementary figures, and 24 supplementary tables. The exact associated manuscript and supplementary document versions are identified by their SHA-256 fingerprints. Data sources include ACEA, FAOSTAT, CWASI, GCAM scenario outputs, USGS irrigation water-use estimates, Kansas irrigation-technology replication data, and complementary water-account datasets. Source-specific citations and attribution requirements are retained in the documentation. Reproduction and validation The documented workflow uses Python 3.11. Separate dependency environments are specified where required. Installing dependencies requires internet access; the numerical analyses use the deposited inputs. Instructions cover the complete workflow and targeted reproduction checks. For version 1.0.1, file checksums, database integrity, and embedded assets were verified. The full-routing analysis was rerun from the deposited GCAM inputs for all 50 future configurations, reproducing the archived global water bounds and joint conservation outcomes within numerical tolerance. This targeted validation does not constitute a new execution of every stage of the study. Interpretation and reuse The modeled water bounds are conditional on specified technology responses, market quantities, supplier availability, production constraints, and water-use coefficients. They are not confidence intervals or globally identified causal effects of irrigation-technology adoption. Future configurations are conditional stress tests, not probabilistic forecasts. Original data compilations and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0, and original analysis code under the MIT License. summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-two entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR) with depth and finds the depth at which it falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: The present study was undertaken to establish pharmacognostic standards and phytochemical profiles of two ethnomedicinally important plants, Cajanus goensis and Sarcostigma kleinii. Both species are traditionally employed in the treatment of rheumatism, inflammatory disorders, and other systemic ailments, yet scientific validation of their crude drug parameters remains limited. Standardization of herbal materials is essential to ensure identity, purity, and reproducibility, thereby reducing variability and enhancing therapeutic reliability. In this study, plant materials were procured from authentic local sources—Cajanus goensis from Udaipur, Rajasthan, and Sarcostigma kleinii from Latur, Maharashtra—and subjected to comprehensive pharmacognostic and phytochemical evaluation. Organoleptic analysis revealed distinct sensory characteristics, with Cajanus goensis exhibiting greenish-brown coloration, earthy odor, and coarse texture, while Sarcostigma kleinii showed yellowish-brown coloration, pungent odor, and oily texture. Macroscopic and microscopic examinations confirmed diagnostic features such as dorsiventral leaves, reticulate venation, thick cuticular layers, and prominent vascular bundles. Physico-chemical evaluation demonstrated that ash values, extractive values, moisture content, and pH were within pharmacopoeial limits, thereby confirming the purity and stability of the crude drugs. Notably, Cajanus goensis exhibited higher alcohol-soluble extractives, while Sarcostigma kleinii showed greater water-soluble extractives, reflecting differences in phytoconstituent solubility. Phytochemical screening revealed the presence of carbohydrates, amino acids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, tannins, and phenolic compounds in both species. Proteins were detected only in Sarcostigma kleinii, while saponins were present exclusively in Cajanus goensis. Sterols were absent in both plants, highlighting unique chemical signatures that aid in authentication. Quantitative estimation confirmed that both species are rich in flavonoids and phenolic compounds, with Sarcostigma kleinii showing slightly higher concentrations (21.06 ± 1.000 mg/g quercetin equivalents and 21.19 ± 0.854 mg/g tannic acid equivalents) compared to Cajanus goensis (19.09 ± 0.444 mg/g and 18.49 ± 0.033 mg/g, respectively). These bioactive constituents are well recognized for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, supporting the traditional use of these plants in rheumatism and related disorders. In conclusion, the study provides reproducible pharmacognostic and phytochemical data for Cajanus goensis and Sarcostigma kleinii, thereby validating their ethnomedicinal claims and establishing a foundation for further pharmacological investigations. The results underscore the importance of standardization in herbal medicine and highlight the potential of these crude drugs as reliable sources of bioactive compounds for future therapeutic applications.
tags: Cajanus goensis; Sarcostigma kleinii; crude drug standardization; phytochemical screening; flavonoids; phenolic compounds; rheumatism; pharmacognosy; herbal medicine; quality control.
title: Standardization And Phytochemical Profiling of Cajanus Goensis and Sarcostigma Kleinii: Establishing Baseline Parameters for Crude Drug Evaluation

summary: What if an AI agent could not complete a consequential action until the real-world result of an earlier, bounded action had been independently verified—and that verification was required to unlock the next execution step? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly operate financial systems, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, autonomous machinery, and critical infrastructure, conventional security mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: authorization establishes what is permitted, but does not necessarily establish what actually happened along the real execution path. Audit logs may record a mistake after its consequences become irreversible. Simulations may succeed while the real destination, network route, transaction system, or physical actuator behaves differently. Even a successful initial authorization does not justify unlimited authority to execute subsequent actions. This paper develops a different architectural principle: “Evidence is the key, not the log.” Building on the distinction that computation is not authority to act , the proposed architecture makes independently validated evidence of a preceding real effect a technical prerequisite for later effectuation. The mechanism is called Receipt-Gated Staged Effectuation , supported by an Interim Effectuation Validator (IEV) . For selected consequential operations, the architecture authorizes a deliberately bounded but real first effect, rather than immediately releasing the complete consequence. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network element, storage component, or hardware controller generates an Effect Confirmation Receipt (ECR) describing what actually occurred. The IEV independently verifies the receipt against the authorized Candidate Act, expected effect, phase, destination, sink identity, freshness, policy, revocation state, and authorized scope. Only after successful validation does the protected domain establish the Continuation Authority Object (CAO) required for the next phase. The critical distinction is that the next effect can be made technically impossible—not merely prohibited by policy—until validated evidence from the preceding real effect becomes available. Possible implementations include receipt-derived cryptographic keys, split-key reconstruction, protected internal state, hardware latches, pre-staged non-executable commands, and pre-delivered ciphertext whose final decryption material remains withheld. Unlike ordinary canary deployment or post-execution monitoring, the earlier phase's evidence becomes part of the causal authority chain. Its receipt is not merely information about the previous operation; it is a required input to the authority enabling the next operation. The paper develops: Three effectuation modes: Direct protected single-phase execution, bounded demonstration followed by full effectuation, and progressive multi-phase execution. Adaptive effectuation: Geometric and risk-dependent progression, reversibility-aware phase sizing, nested stages, and parallel effectuation. Cryptographic causal dependency: Receipt-derived execution material, split credentials, tokenless continuation, hardware-gated enablement, and protected state transitions. Protected evidence semantics: Proof of delivery versus proof of effect, negative receipts, receipt freshness, destination binding, cross-device protection, Merkle receipt structures, and privacy-preserving confirmation. Independent continuation authority: Human, automatic, hybrid, and multi-authority decisions separated from the potentially compromised AI-agent environment. Fail-closed recovery: Missing or conflicting receipts, uncertain outcomes, replay protection, atomic consumption, reconciliation, and prevention of blind retries. Anti-bypass enforcement: Protected execution boundaries, credential surrogation, taint and provenance controls, alternative-path closure, and software–hardware implementation ind
title: Evidence Is the Key, Not the Log: Cryptographic Execution Control for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems

summary: A book in progress on agentic coding and agentic research, compiled from the repository that is its evidence, written around one problem: moving the expensive kernels of the WAVEWATCH III (WW3) third-generation spectral wind-wave model to GPUs without changing the answer. summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a comment on a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview and comments at https://prereview.org/reviews/22745390 . Thank you, Evgenii, for the detailed and constructive PREreview. Your comments led us to substantially strengthen both the experimental design and the interpretation of the results. We have now released a revised version of the manuscript that addresses the main points raised in the review. The revision includes: A 30-seed robustness analysis rather than relying on a single simulation seed A correlation sweep for estimator errors from ρ = 0 to 0.8 Regression-fitted and test-set oracle aggregation baselines Shared-noise experiments for the model–collective calibration signal, reported with ROC-AUC and lift Explicit specification of the four-Wave rolling calibration window, software versions, and PCG64 RNG Portfolio scaling to 100 Feature Blocks using an exact binary MILP reference An explicit separation between budget-constrained portfolio selection and ODP's native dependency-aware sequencing role An exact and scaling benchmark for ODP sequencing under prerequisite constraints An explicit competing-interest disclosure A public reproducibility package containing the simulation code, deterministic seeds, generated data, analysis scripts, and validation material. One particularly useful outcome of the revision was that the stronger experiments narrowed some of our original claims. For example, inverse-MSE aggregation performs very strongly when estimator errors are independent, but its advantage collapses under strong shared error. We also found that ODP distance is not the strongest heuristic for budget-constrained portfolio selection, while it performs very differently in its native sequencing role, where ERS/BVS is exactly optimal for the declared objective without dependencies and remains close to the exact optimum under the tested prerequisite constraints. Revised manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10648 Reproducibility package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23261325 Thank you again for the review. It improved the paper.
